passages.t: ‘Out of the depths I cry to You, O LORD’, and ‘with You there is forgiveness’
passages.happening:
Psalm 130 begins at the bottom. “A song of ascents. Out of the depths I cry to You, O LORD!” (verse 1). “O Lord, hear my voice; let Your ears be attentive to my plea for mercy” (verse 2).

The singer knows what is wrong, and part of it is himself. “If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand?” (verse 3). If God kept a record of every wrong, no one could stand before him.

Then the turn. “But with You there is forgiveness, so that You may be feared” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
‘The depths’ are deep waters, the Old Testament picture of being overwhelmed, close to drowning and to death. Another psalm says, “I have drifted into deep waters, where the flood engulfs me” (Psalm 69:2). The singer does not say what put him there. But verse 3 suggests that his own sin is part of the weight.

Notice verse 3. It is a confession for everyone, not only for the singer. No one could stand. That is why the book page, in its part on whether the psalmists claim to be sinless, points to this verse.

Verse 4 surprises. You might expect: with you there is forgiveness, so that we need not fear you. Instead it says ‘so that You may be feared’. ‘Fear’ here means awe and worship, as the note on Psalm 111 explains. A God who only kept records would drive people away in despair. A God who forgives draws them near in wonder.

Christians have long counted this psalm among the seven ‘penitential psalms’, prayers of sorrow for sin, a grouping known since at least the sixth century. It is often called by its first words in Latin, De profundis, ‘out of the depths’. Martin Luther made it into a German hymn, first printed in 1524. The note on Psalm 120 explains the Songs of Ascents.
passages.later:
John wrote, “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). Paul wrote that “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified freely by His grace” (Romans 3:23-24).

And for those who belong to Christ: “Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).
passages.asks:
Have you ever felt that your wrongs were too many to be forgiven? Verse 3 agrees that, if God kept score, no one would stand. Verse 4 says he does not keep score that way. With him there is forgiveness.

You may pray verse 1 from wherever you are. ‘The depths’ are not too deep for God to hear.

passages.t: ‘More than watchmen wait for the morning’
passages.happening:
Now the singer waits. “I wait for the LORD; my soul does wait, and in His word I put my hope” (verse 5). “My soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning” (verse 6), and he says the last words twice over.

Then he turns from himself to the whole people. “O Israel, put your hope in the LORD, for with the LORD is loving devotion, and with Him is redemption in abundance” (verse 7). “And He will redeem Israel from all iniquity” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Watchmen stood on the city walls, or in the temple, through the night. Their work was to stay awake in the dark. Their watch ended only with the dawn. There were no street lights, and the night was long. A first hearer knew how a watchman longed for the first grey light in the east.

The singer says he waits for God more than that. And he says it twice. The repeated line sounds like a man counting the hours.

‘Wait’ in the Psalms is not idle. The book page explains the word: looking to God in hope. And the hope here rests on two things: God's ‘word’, his promise (verse 5), and his ‘loving devotion’, his hesed, the love that keeps its promises (verse 7).

The psalm ends with the widest hope of all. Not just one person forgiven, but a whole people redeemed ‘from all iniquity’. Redemption ‘in abundance’ means more than enough.
passages.later:
Simeon was an old man in Jerusalem who “was waiting for the consolation of Israel” (Luke 2:25). He held the baby Jesus in his arms in the temple.

The angel told Joseph to name Mary's son Jesus, “because He will save His people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). Paul wrote, “In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses” (Ephesians 1:7).
passages.hard: If ‘the depths’ describe your life now, and the night feels long, please do not carry it alone. The man who prayed this psalm was still waiting when it ended. Waiting is not a failure of faith. Tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor or a friend. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks:
What are you waiting for? Psalm 130 does not promise when the morning comes. It promises that it will, because God's love keeps its word.

And notice that the singer does not keep his hope to himself. In verse 7 he turns to others: ‘O Israel, put your hope in the LORD.’ When you have found hope in the depths, pass it on.
